text: Define a typed file and directory change-notification Operation (inotify/fanotify replacement) and its Linux-personality bridge, required by IDEs at V1.
Define the durability contract of Write and StorageTransaction (the point at which data is power-loss safe) and prove it with a fault-injected power-cut test on NVMe.
Provide storage quotas per user and per ResourceDomain with settings UI, distinct from content-store garbage collection.
Provide disk health: TRIM/discard policy, SMART monitoring, checksum-scrub error reporting UX, and filesystem repair from the recovery environment.
Provide encrypted, snapshot-based, scheduled user-data backup to external or network targets as the counterpart of machine-to-machine restore.
Exclude GPLv2-incompatible filesystems such as CDDL ZFS from in-kernel use in the filesystem choice ADR.
rationale: An otherwise attractive storage backend would make the kernel undistributable.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Apply block- or file-level verity (dm-verity/fs-verity style) to the immutable system store with its root hash carried in the signed generation manifest, completing the chain from firmware to userspace binaries.
rationale: §26 asks for checksums but a checksum without a signed root is integrity, not authenticity; 1.0 needs a verifiable chain of trust.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the encryption layering relative to the content-addressed store and system generations: whether the immutable, publicly known system store is verified-but-unencrypted while user and application data are encrypted, and how deduplication interacts with encryption.
rationale: Encrypting deduplicated content-addressed objects changes both the deduplication ratio and what an attacker learns from ciphertext, so it must be a deliberate choice.

text: Desktop search and indexing service that indexes only content the user has granted, exposes typed search over files, apps, settings and semantic interfaces, and powers the launcher.
rationale: The launcher search and the AI action graph in §44 both need an index, and an indexer with ambient home-directory access would violate §9.

text: Trash and undo-delete semantics built on storage snapshots, plus removable-media automount, safe eject, and MTP device access granted through the file chooser.
rationale: Users expect a recycle bin and USB sticks to just work, and both are natural applications of the CoW storage model.

text: Network file share providers (SMB, NFS, WebDAV, SFTP) surfaced as storage objects in the file chooser and file browser with credentials in the secrets service.
rationale: Home NAS and office shares are a common adoption blocker and belong in the storage provider model rather than ad hoc mounts.

text: Decide the on-disk partition and volume layout for generations, content-addressed store, user data, swap/hibernate and recovery, including registered GPT partition type GUIDs.
rationale: Layout must be fixed before V0.5 generations exist, and foreign tools (GParted, Windows Disk Management) must be able to identify JakeOS partitions unambiguously.

text: Retain the in-kernel NTFS read/write driver with a policy for dirty volumes, missing chkdsk, and Windows permission/ACL mapping into the native storage layer.
rationale: Dual-boot users and external drives from Windows machines are NTFS-formatted; read-only support is insufficient for a shared data partition.

text: Support exFAT and FAT32 for removable media including formatting, safe eject, and the timestamp/character-set limitations of each.
rationale: Cameras, SD cards, USB sticks and console storage are exFAT by industry agreement.

text: Decide how the capability-based storage model degrades on foreign filesystems lacking its metadata: xattr fallback, case-insensitivity, forbidden characters, timestamp precision and permission bits.
rationale: Native Collections on NTFS or exFAT must behave predictably or users lose metadata silently when copying across volumes.

text: Removable and foreign volumes are surfaced as user-consented, capability-scoped collections rather than ambient mounts, and appear under conventional /media and drive-letter paths only inside personalities.
rationale: Plugging in a USB stick is where ambient authority typically re-enters a capability system; the policy must exist before V2 hardware work.

text: Unlock and mount LUKS, ext4, Btrfs and XFS volumes from other Linux installations, and decide whether BitLocker volumes are readable via dislocker-style user-space support.
rationale: Reading the previous OS's encrypted disk is a prerequisite for in-place migration.

text: Define a native storage-provider interface so cloud storage (OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud) appears as capability-scoped collections with on-demand hydration, and decide which providers ship in 1.0.
rationale: Migrating users' files increasingly live in cloud sync services rather than on disk.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Benchmark candidate filesystems (btrfs, bcachefs, ZFS, XFS with reflink) for snapshot creation, clone, checksum overhead, dedup and crash consistency, and choose the initial storage substrate.
rationale: System generations and dev environment snapshots depend on the substrate and migrating user data between filesystems later is a 1.0-blocking risk.

text: Retain Linux NVMe support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux SATA support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux mature filesystem implementations in the forked kernel.
Paths are not the security model; no native authority check may be based on a filesystem path.
Preserve Linux NVMe support as the storage mechanism underneath native storage objects.
ADR: replace the global filesystem namespace with per-component capability-scoped storage objects.
Storage is a user-space service above native kernel objects.
Preserve Linux storage drivers in the fork initially.
Preserve mature Linux filesystems (ext4, btrfs, xfs, vfat) in the fork initially.
Define Object<File>.
Define Object<Directory>.
Define the temporary-storage capability that a launched application receives (scratch storage scoped to the component).
The OS-owned chooser returns a Capability<Image, ReadWrite> for the object the user selected.
Selecting one file must never require granting access to the containing directory (e.g. ~/Pictures).
MemoryObject supports the persistent property (backed by durable storage).
Resolve semantics of persistent MemoryObjects: relation to the storage model, crash consistency, and content addressing.
The kernel must support a StorageTransaction Operation kind that atomically applies a group of storage changes and completes on commit or abort.
Humans must continue to see files and folders in the user-facing storage model.
Native applications must not receive a universal filesystem namespace by default.
The kernel or storage service must expose File as a typed object accessible only via Capability<File, Rights>.
The storage model must expose Directory as a typed object whose capability scopes access to its subtree.
The storage model must expose Collection as a typed object representing a user-meaningful group of items (e.g. a photo album) independent of directory layout.
The storage model must expose Blob as a typed immutable byte object, preferably content-addressed (cross-ref §27).
The storage model must expose ApplicationData as per-application private persistent storage granted by default without user prompt.
The storage model must expose UserSelected<T> as the type of objects returned by an OS chooser, carrying the granted authority.
Write a verification test that an application using files.choose<Image>() can read the chosen image while holding no capability to /home/<user>/Pictures or any directory.
Decide how the type parameter of choose<T> (Image, Document, Directory) maps to content types and how the chooser filters and validates selections.
Define the save-as flow: how an application obtains authority to create a new file in a user-chosen location without directory access.
Storage must support copy-on-write semantics for files and objects.
Storage must support snapshots of subtrees and of the whole system volume.
Storage must support deduplication of identical content.
Storage must support checksums on data and metadata with detection of corruption on read.
Storage must support immutable versions of objects that cannot be modified once sealed.
Storage must support cheap clones (reflink) of files and trees.
Storage must support atomic replacement of a file or tree so readers never observe a partial update.
Storage must support transactions grouping multiple changes with all-or-nothing commit (backs StorageTransaction Operation in §18).
Storage must support integrity verification of stored objects against expected content hashes on demand and at boot for system generations.
Decide the initial underlying Linux filesystem for the native storage layer (btrfs, bcachefs, ZFS, XFS with reflink plus overlay) against the nine storage requirements.
Do not write a new filesystem merely because the OS is new; the initial implementation must sit over a mature Linux filesystem.
Define the criteria (semantic gaps, measured performance shortfalls) under which a native filesystem or object store would be justified, and re-evaluate at each milestone gate.
Build the native storage service as a user-space component that mediates capability-scoped access to the underlying filesystem (cross-ref §4 User Services: Storage).
Immutable data must be identifiable by content hash using an identifier form such as sha256:<hex>.
Decide the content-hash algorithm and identifier format (SHA-256 vs BLAKE3, multihash prefix, chunking scheme for large objects) and its upgrade path.
Build a content-addressed object store service that stores, retrieves, and reference-counts immutable objects by hash.
The content-addressed store must deduplicate identical objects across packages, generations, and caches.
The content-addressed store must verify integrity by recomputing hashes on ingest and on verification requests.
Caches (build outputs, decoded assets, precompiled code) must be keyed by content hash so cached results are safe to reuse.
Define garbage collection for the content-addressed store: root set (live generations, installed packages, pinned objects), collection policy, and user control.
Decide how the content-addressed store maps onto the chosen filesystem (hardlinked object directory, reflinked files, filesystem-native dedup) to avoid double storage.
Restore must be able to revert user data via storage snapshots (cross-ref §26).
Define how configuration and application state are captured as versioned objects so they can participate in restore (structured settings store vs snapshotting ApplicationData).
Resolve how file.type is determined for automation conditions (typed object kinds vs MIME sniffing) and where the type registry lives (§25 UserSelected<T>).
Resolve where typed object kinds such as Image come from (a platform type registry) so files.choose::<Image>() and UserSelected<T> share one type system.
Do not invent a new filesystem immediately; build storage semantics over a mature Linux filesystem first (cross-ref §26).
Basic capability-based file selection: OS-owned chooser returning Capability<File> to the requesting application (cross-ref §25).
User-visible snapshots of user data and application state with browse and restore.
Principle 8: human-facing files and folders remain without making paths the security model.
